10.0.0.en: 1 "My soul is weary of my life; I will leave my complaint upon myself; I will speak in the bitterness of my soul. 2 I will say unto God, Do not condemn me; shew me wherefore thou contendest with me. 3 Is it good unto thee that thou shouldest oppress, that thou shouldest despise the work of thine hands, and shine upon the counsel of the wicked? 4 Hast thou eyes of flesh? or seest thou as man seeth? 5 Are thy days as the days of man? are thy years as man's days, 6 That thou enquirest after mine iniquity, and searchest after my sin? 7 Thou knowest that I am not wicked; and there is none that can deliver out of thine hand.

10.0.1.en: "My soul is weary of my life."

10.0.2.en: "I will leave my complaint upon myself; I will speak in the bitterness of my soul" [1].

10.0.3.en: With some courage Job stands before the Judge to raise his complaint to the One who passed sentence on him to enter into bitter afflictions. Job the tempted man realized that there is no way to complain about what had befallen him, by God's permission, except to raise it to God Himself.

10.0.4.en: Job was unable to defend himself before God, for he feared His greatness and found no one to reconcile him to Him. Then he cried out: "My soul is weary of my life." In despair he longed for death.

10.0.5.en: Job let loose his complaint against himself; he does not accuse God of injustice and cruelty, but accuses himself of ignorance, not knowing the basis of the dispute, for Job supposed that the fault was in him, yet he does not know it.

10.0.6.en: He did not want to utter a word, lest he sin, but the bitterness within him burst forth and spoke. As the Apostle says, "sin that dwelleth in me" (Rom 7:20).

10.0.7.en: * [My soul is anxious concerning my life] [1]. Now that the present life has begun to become tasteless and the love of the Creator to become sweet, the soul is kindled against itself, and accuses itself of the sins that it formerly justified, as it was ignorant of heavenly things. Therefore he continues: [I will let loose my words against myself] [1].

10.0.9.en: * Let your sufferings be books that counsel you.

10.0.10.en: St. Ephrem the Syrian. Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that righteous Job, in the midst of severe trials, lifted his heart toward heavenly things, and his heart was kindled with love toward God. Then the sins that he had not felt before, or had regarded as trivial or justified, became clear to him; therefore he loathed what his life had been, and became the accuser of himself, allowing himself to utter his complaint against himself.

10.0.11.en: Job became a judge of himself, so as not to fall under condemnation on the great day of the Lord, which would find him guilty. He prefers to condemn himself before God condemns him, even in this world, lest his enemies mock him when God hands him over to them for his discipline. Truly, how sweet it is for a man to lay the blame on himself!

10.0.12.en: Thus affliction is turned from a weight that embitters the soul into an enjoyment of the weight of eternal glories, which we experience in the midst of sufferings. Therefore the Apostle Paul says: "For our light affliction, which is but for a moment, worketh for us a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory" (2 Cor 4:17).

10.0.13.en: * "I will speak in the bitterness of my soul." He who tells of his sins, loathing them, must speak in the bitterness of his soul, so that the bitterness itself may punish the accusations of his tongue in justifying his conscience. But we must keep in mind that it brings a kind of security from the pains of compunction, which deals a blow to itself, and then it rises with greater confidence to face the interrogation of the heavenly Judge.

10.0.15.en: * The soul does not return to God unless it is torn away from the world, and nothing rightly tears it away but toil and pain.

10.0.16.en: St. Augustine. * The nature of the Apostle Paul was not different from our nature; nor was his soul different from our souls; nor did he live in another world, but dwelt in the same world and city and was subject to the same laws and customs, yet he surpassed in virtue all men, past and present. Now where are those who object to the difficulty of virtue and the ease of sin? This man condemns them by his words: "For our light affliction, which is but for a moment, worketh for us a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory" (2 Cor 4:17). If his afflictions were bearable and light, how much more ours, which, if you compare them, become nothing or mere pleasures...?

10.0.17.en: Paul embraced sufferings with love and without reward, and bore with all joy the difficulties and obstacles he met on the road of virtue. He was not troubled by weakness of the body, or the pressures of responsibility, or the tyranny of habits, or anything else. Moreover, his responsibilities surpassed all the tasks of leaders and kings, yet he grew in virtue daily. The increase of dangers became a cause for his zeal to be kindled all the more, and he said: "Forgetting those things which are behind, and reaching forth unto those things which are before" (Phil 3:13).

10.0.18.en: When death drew near to him, he called everyone to share this joy with him, saying: "For the same cause also do ye joy, and rejoice with me" (Phil 2:18). He exulted with joy in affliction and pain and in every humiliation. He wrote to the Corinthians: [Therefore I take pleasure in infirmities, in reproaches, in necessities, in persecutions, in distresses for Christ's sake] (2 Cor 12:10). And he called these the weapons of righteousness, showing that they are a fruitful source of benefit to him, so that he became invincible before his enemies. And in spite of beatings, persecution, and insults, he was like one at a joyful wedding, correcting many concepts of victory, rejoicing, giving thanks to God, saying: "Now thanks be unto God, which always causeth us to triumph in Christ" (2 Cor 2:14).

10.0.19.en: * How glorious are sufferings! By them we are made like His death!

10.0.20.en: As the refiner of gold casts the piece of gold into the furnace to endure the fire for a time until he sees that it has been purified, so God permits humanity to be tested by afflictions until it is purified and gains great benefit... Let us not be troubled or despair when trials come upon us. For just as the refiner of gold knows the time when the gold should be left in the furnace, and brings it out at the appointed time, and does not leave it any longer in the fire lest it be spoiled and burned, how much more does God know this. So when He sees that we have been purified all the more, He frees us from our trials lest we be cast down and cast out because of the increase of our evils.

10.0.21.en: When something happens to us that we did not expect, let us not murmur nor let our hearts faint, but let us endure God, who knows these things exactly, so that He may test our hearts with fire as it pleases Him, since He does this with the aim of benefiting those who are tried. Therefore the wise man commands us to submit to God in all things, because He knows perfectly when to bring us out of the furnace of evil. (Sir 1:1, 2)

10.0.22.en: Let us submit to Him always, and thank Him continually, enduring everything with contentment, whether He grants us blessings or offers us chastenings. For the latter are a kind of blessing.

10.0.23.en: For the physician is not only one who allows us to bathe (in the baths)... or to go to pleasant gardens, but also when he uses the scalpel and the knife he is a physician!

10.0.24.en: And a father is not only when he caresses his son, but also when he disciplines and punishes him... he is a father!

10.0.25.en: And since we know that God is more compassionate than all physicians, we are not to inquire into His dealings, nor demand an account from Him of them, but let Him do what is good in His eyes. We do not distinguish whether He frees us from the trial or disciplines us, because by both ways He desires to restore us to health and make us partners with Him; and He knows our different needs, and what suits each one of us, and how and in what way we must be saved.

10.0.26.en: Let us follow Him wherever He commands us, and not think much whether He commands us to walk an easy and smooth road or a hard and rough one.

10.0.27.en: St. John Chrysostom. "I will say unto God, Do not condemn me."

10.1.0.en: "Shew me wherefore thou contendest with me" [2].

10.1.1.en: Despite what appears in Job as murmuring, he declares his ignorance of the secret of the dispute and condemns himself, although he does not know what his offense is. Therefore in humility he asks: "Do not condemn me," that is, do not separate me from You.

10.1.2.en: Since You have permitted me to bear sufferings, do not permit sin, the cause of my weariness, to settle within me.

10.1.3.en: Since You have permitted me the rod of discipline, do not permit my destruction.

10.1.4.en: Discipline me, but do not judge me worthy of condemnation. As the Apostle says: "But when we are judged, we are chastened of the Lord, that we should not be condemned with the world" (1 Cor 11:32).

10.1.5.en: What Job desired was fulfilled in Christ Jesus: "There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus, who walk not after the flesh, but after the Spirit" (Rom 8:1).

10.1.6.en: God permits trials so that the believer may cry out, asking for knowledge and the discovery of the mysteries of God: [Make me understand; do not contend with me].

10.1.7.en: Through affliction righteous Job realized that he was a sinner, but this is not enough for him; he wants God to grant him understanding to realize what his sin is, so that he may confess it to God and flee from it through divine grace.

10.1.8.en: * Great is faith, and great is the power of conscience, that a man should call God as a witness to the fulfillment of his aim.

10.1.9.en: Job did not reject what befell him through his human condition, but rejects what comes from unholiness, confessing that it befalls him out of weakness.

10.1.10.en: That a man sins is from his human condition, for no one is exempt from falling.

10.1.11.en: But that he should act in an unholy way is not from his human condition; it is the poison of unbelief through the evil heart.

10.1.12.en: It is not fitting for the righteous man to do this.

10.1.13.en: Forgiveness for man depends on the mercies of God, not on the power of man.

10.1.14.en: St. Ambrose. * [Saying to God: Do not condemn me, make me understand why You contend with me?] [2]. In declaring himself a sinner, [in the bitterness of his soul], what does he say to God except that he asks not to be condemned, since the bitterness of his present compunction removes the pains of wrath from his sins?

10.1.15.en: God judges man in this life in two ways: by recognizing that through present troubles he has already begun to bring upon himself the torments to come, or else by lifting the torments to come through the present blows...

10.1.16.en: Discipline delivers from woe only those who change. But those who are not reformed by present troubles enter into other troubles as a result.

10.1.17.en: If some present punishments did not preserve from eternal woe, Paul would not say: "But when we are judged, we are chastened of the Lord, that we should not be condemned with the world" (1 Cor 11:32). As it was said to John by the voice of the angel: "As many as I love, I rebuke and chasten" (Rev 3:19), as it is written: "For whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth, and scourgeth every son whom he receiveth" (Heb 12:6)...

10.1.18.en: Rightly it is said here: [Make me understand, why do You judge me?] [2]. As though he were saying plainly: You have exercised Your judgment upon me by Your blows upon me, so that by these blows You may make me secure from condemnation.

10.1.19.en: This statement can also be understood in another sense. Often the righteous man receives the blows of trial, and as he examines his life with the skillful eye that questions him, he cannot determine precisely for what sin he was struck, even though he feels in himself that he is a sinner. He is all the more terrified under the rod because of his ignorance of the true reason for the blows. He prays to the Judge to show him the purpose of His striking him, so that he may be disciplined by weeping over his sin. For he is fully certain that the righteous Avenger will not grieve anyone unjustly. And that he has been placed under the scourges as a grave warning, and yet he could not discover of himself what he ought to grieve over.

10.2.0.en: "Is it good unto thee that thou shouldest oppress, that thou shouldest despise the work of thine hands, and shine upon the counsel of the wicked?" [3]

10.2.1.en: Job returned to reproach God like one who feels wronged, since He lets the wicked carry out their evil counsel in the lives of His believers, who are the work of His hands.

10.2.2.en: It is clear throughout the whole book that Job did not ascribe injustice to God, but he was in great perplexity, for he did not know how to interpret the events, in spite of his awareness and certainty of God's providence.

10.2.3.en: When man in his weakness concentrates on the afflictions that have come upon him, he wonders how God leaves the wicked to carry out their evil counsels against the children of God. Man thinks as though God had forgotten that he is the work of His hands and the object of His care, and that He has left the wicked to do what they want.

10.2.4.en: But when the believer lifts his eyes to God, he realizes that He is the good heavenly Physician who turns the counsels of the wicked into the edification and glory of His children. He permits them to inflict affliction, but He gives His children the power of patience and endurance. God will not permit a trial beyond the strength and capacities of His believers! Rightly we sing, saying: "The LORD hath broken the staff of the wicked, and the sceptre of the rulers" (Isa 14:5).

10.2.5.en: * The Lord did not [shine upon the counsel of the wicked] in a way that would restrain the soul of the righteous, even when he hands over his body to the arts of their testing of him... But the sharpness of their counsel becomes nothing, since the Creator adjusts the blows according to our ability to endure...

10.2.6.en: Paul said well: "But God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that ye are able; but will with the temptation also make a way to escape, that ye may be able to bear it" (1 Cor 10:13). If the merciful God allowed trials beyond our power, certainly there would be no man able to stand before the cunning schemes of the evil spirits without falling to the ground.

10.2.7.en: * He fittingly adds: "the work of thine hands," as though saying frankly: You will not press with hard cruelty on one whom You remember You created by Your grace.

10.2.9.en: * He did not say: "Why do You disown the righteous man, the virtuous man," but "the work of thine hands."

10.2.10.en: St. John Chrysostom. * [You shine upon the counsel of the wicked]; if it is because of my sins (that You discipline me), how do You regard their counsel?

10.2.11.en: * Truly the righteous suffer at the present time within certain limits, and at the present time the wicked oppress the righteous. How? Sometimes the wicked reach worldly positions, and become judges or kings. God does this to discipline His flock, to discipline His people... But He does not leave the rod thus. For the rod of the wicked is left for a time upon the lot of the righteous, but it is not left forever.

10.2.12.en: St. Augustine. * "As the mountains are round about Jerusalem, so the LORD is round about his people from henceforth even for ever" (Ps 125:2)... He says: if even mountains fortify it, it still needs fortification from the Lord to be impregnable... It is not for her to trust in a chain of mountains.

10.2.13.en: What makes it fortified, see this: [For the rod of the wicked shall not rest upon the lot of the righteous] (Ps 125:3). He points to a fitting reason for obtaining the Lord's help, so as to encourage them to trust in Him. What is it? The Psalmist says: He would not bear that the goodness of the righteous be in the hands of sinners...

10.2.14.en: He does not permit them to gain authority over the inheritance of the righteous; and if He permits it, it is only for a time, for their correction, counsel, and discipline.

10.3.0.en: St. John Chrysostom. "Hast thou eyes of flesh? or seest thou as man seeth?" [4]

10.3.1.en: Job was confident that God's eyes are not like the bodily eyes of men; He sees in the dark and knows hidden things; His eyes are in every place (Prov 15:3), and run to and fro throughout the whole earth (2 Chr 16:9). Everything is open before God. Therefore the Apostle says: "But we are sure that the judgment of God is according to truth" (Rom 2:2).

10.3.2.en: Since God is aware of the secrets of Job's heart, and knows his love for Him and the purity of his heart, He has no need to permit the enemy to tempt him in order that he may be proved before the Lord.

10.3.3.en: Truly God had no need to hand Job over to temptation in order to examine his depths; rather He permitted it to put the enemy of good to shame, and that Job might be proved all the more through his patience and endurance with thanksgiving, without blaspheming God.

10.3.4.en: In plain reproach Job tells God that His eyes are not like the eyes of men; they search the depths of man without limit, and know even what he will do in the future, so what need is there to examine him? He asks Him not to hand him over to the wicked one, lest he press upon him and he sin.

10.3.5.en: * "Hast thou eyes of flesh? or seest thou as man seeth?" [4]... The eyes of the flesh cannot look at the works of the ages except within a certain limit of time; moreover the days and years of men differ from the days and years of eternity. Our life begins in time and ends in time, while eternity is without limits...

10.3.7.en: * "Or seest thou as man seeth?" These words mean... You have no need to examine Job and look closely at him to see whether he is as the enemy claims, for as You are God You know him beforehand. You do not look as a mortal looks, so why was I handed over to the enemy so that he might force me to commit iniquity?

10.4.0.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem. "Are thy days as the days of man? are thy years as man's days" [5].

10.4.1.en: As God is unlimited, His days are unlimited; He is the Creator of time. The days of man, as Jacob said to Pharaoh, are [few and evil], subject to change. Therefore God's view of things and His judgments differ from man's view. For God the past is as the present and the future; all is present before Him.

10.5.0.en: "That thou enquirest after mine iniquity, and searchest after my sin?" [6]

10.5.1.en: Job sees that God is too great to enquire after his sin or search after his iniquity, or that Job in his own eyes is too insignificant for God to be occupied with him to search out his sins. It is as though he says with the prophet Jeremiah: "We acknowledge, O LORD, our wickedness, and the iniquity of our fathers: for we have sinned against thee. Do not abhor us, for thy name's sake, do not disgrace the throne of thy glory" (Jer 14:20-21).

10.5.2.en: * It is as though he says, questioning in humility: Why do You examine me by blows in time, when even before time existed You knew me fully within Yourself? Why do You hold an inquiry about my sins through blows, when by the power of Your eternity You knew me before You created me?

10.6.0.en: "Thou knowest that I am not wicked; and there is none that can deliver out of thine hand" [7].

10.6.1.en: He had already confessed that he is a sinner, but he is not a wicked obstinate man who resists God and His commandment, nor a hypocrite. Therefore he says: "Thou knowest that I am not wicked."

10.6.2.en: So it is fitting for us to confess that we are sinners, yet by grace we declare to Him with the Apostle: "Thou knowest that I love thee" (Jn 21:17).

10.6.3.en: Although I confess that I am wicked, there is none to deliver me out of Your hand but You! To You I flee, so do not be angry with me!

10.6.4.en: * [There is none that can escape out of Your hand]; it is as though he says plainly: What is left for You but to forgive, You whose power no man can resist? For just as there is no one who enjoys Your visitation by his own merit and loftiness, so it is Your compassion that allows the obtaining of forgiveness.

10.6.6.en: * Even if You bear witness for me, I cannot be saved by my righteousness, and when You wish to strike me I cannot save myself, because [who can deliver me out of Your hands?] All creation is in the right hand of Him who has eternal glory.

10.7.s.en: 2. His life in the hand of God

10.7.0.en: 8 "Thine hands have made me and fashioned me together round about; yet thou dost destroy me. 9 Remember, I beseech thee, that thou hast made me as the clay; and wilt thou bring me into dust again? 10 Hast thou not poured me out as milk, and curdled me like cheese? 11 Thou hast clothed me with skin and flesh, and hast fenced me with bones and sinews. 12 Thou hast granted me life and favour, and thy visitation hath preserved my spirit. 13 And these things hast thou hid in thine heart: I know that this is with thee:

10.7.1.en: "Thine hands have made me and fashioned me together round about."

10.7.3.en: Man owes his existence to God, but when a trial comes upon him he sees as though God wants to swallow him up.

10.7.4.en: Many of the Church Fathers used this passage to answer the followers of Mani and others who claimed that the human body is an element of darkness, and that it is corrupt by nature and must be gotten rid of.

10.7.5.en: St. Jacob of Serugh sees that the body cannot live alone, nor can the soul live alone. [The body was not granted permanent life without the soul, and the soul was not granted sensation without the body. The life of the soul is lifeless without the body, and the body laid in the dust remains without life.]

10.7.6.en: Many Fathers of the Church pointed out that one of the blessings of the divine Incarnation is that God restored dignity to the body which He created, for the eternal Word of God did not disdain to bear a true human body and to perform bodily acts.

10.7.7.en: * Because the Word came down and came to be flesh with those of flesh, He walked in the way of all who are born, and remained in the world thirty years in humility. Then He began to act with the power of His might.

10.7.8.en: It is wonderful that He dwelt in the carpenter's house, mingled with them, and lived according to their custom...

10.7.9.en: The wonder is that the heavens are full of His glorification, and He was content with a small house in which to be brought up...!

10.7.10.en: He became a child and nursed milk and did not tire... He became a boy and measured the markets with His steps... He became a youth and worshiped in the carpenter's house. He became a man and bowed His head before John, and with the penitents He went down to be baptized in His humility...

10.7.11.en: Let us believe that He came and became flesh, not in appearance but in truth. He became man so that the world might feel that the second Adam had shown Himself to renew the world in place of the first, whom the serpent bit.

10.7.12.en: Had He begun to perform mighty works from His youth, they would have wronged Him, saying that He had not truly become incarnate, and that His body was an illusion and was not a body. For this reason our Lord waited thirty years, and then began to walk in the way of mighty works, so that in the body He might be a perfect man like Adam. For He went out to contend with the enemy (Satan) in place of Adam.

10.7.13.en: St. Jacob of Serugh. * We do not want to be rid of the body, but of the corruption in it. Our body is a burden to us, not because it is a body, but because it is corrupt and subject to pain. But when the new life comes, it removes this corruption; I say this corruption, not the body itself.

10.7.14.en: * If you wish to learn what kind of body God made at first, let us go to Paradise and look for the man who was created in the beginning. That body was neither corrupt nor dead. Rather it was like a golden statue coming out of the furnace shining with splendor, its frame free from all corruption. Work did not make it weary; no sweat poured from it. Nothing plotted against it, nor was anything of the kind found to trouble it.

10.7.15.en: St. John Chrysostom. * How great was this saint's grief for the common weakness of all men! How severe is the providence that God made man with His hands! Iniquity may be excused on the plea of (human) weakness, and grace declares its eternal work in us through the tenderness of heavenly protection.

10.7.16.en: St. Ambrose. * [Thy hands have made me and fashioned me together round about; yet thou dost suddenly cast me down] [8]. It is as though he says to Him in humility: Even if what I do is unfit to satisfy You if it is subjected to a just examination, remember Your mercy, lest the work of Your hands perish... Why do You thus slight me, when You created me in such circumstances of honor?

10.7.18.en: * [You have struck me] not as a judge, but as a father who corrects me!

10.7.19.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem. What does he mean by the hands of God?

10.7.20.en: * Since we read that the Holy Spirit is the finger of God (Lk 11:20), we reckon that the fingers refer to the Son and the Spirit. Finally, to indicate that he holds sanctification from both the Son and the Spirit, a certain saint says: "Thine hands have made me and fashioned me" (Job 10:8).

10.7.21.en: St. Ambrose. * [Thy hands have made me and formed me]. It refers to the divine providence that works after our creation.

10.7.22.en: Theodoret, Bishop of Cyrus. "Remember, I beseech thee, that thou hast made me as the clay."

10.8.0.en: "And wilt thou bring me into dust again?" [9]

10.8.1.en: Job resorts to God's surpassing love for man. God raised him from clay and gave him all these surpassing capacities; will God turn back from His love and return man to what he was?

10.8.2.en: Man must not boast because he was formed from clay, and at the same time he must not belittle himself or despise his life, for he is the work of God, who created him in His image and likeness.

10.8.3.en: * Job seems to say: Remember the weakness of the flesh, and forgive my iniquity.

10.8.5.en: * Why do You forget Your work? Why do You forget Your visitation?

10.8.6.en: Yes, why do You forget my weakness?

10.8.7.en: For what is man but Your visiting him? (Ps 8:4; Heb 2:6).

10.8.8.en: Therefore do not forget him who is weak. Remember, O Lord, that You created me weak; remember that You formed me as the clay (Ps 103:14; Job 10:9). How can I stand unless Your providence continually directs me to strengthen this clay, so that my strength comes forth from Your face? [Thou hidest thy face, they are troubled] (Ps 104:29).

10.8.9.en: * The needs of the body generate concerns and bring us into pursuits that hinder the soul's strength and prevent its concentration. Saint Job explained this well: [Remember that you have made me of clay] (Job 10:9). If the body is clay, then surely it defiles us and does not cleanse us. It corrupts the soul and defiles it by excess in satisfying passion. "Thou hast clothed me with skin and flesh, and hast fenced me with bones and sinews" (Job 10:11). Thus our souls are bound and tormented by the sinews of the body, and at times become hardened, often when they bow down. "Do not release me from my sin. If I am wicked, woe is me! If I am righteous, I dare not lift up my head, for I am full of dishonor. You bring tortures against me" (Job 10:14-15, 17) LXX.

10.8.10.en: St. Ambrose. * (Man) is placed in the hand of God (Ps 31:6), who is a safe harbor (Ps 107:30) and a strong tower (Ps 61:3); by nature He is merciful, rescuing and saving. God takes care of those whom He made from clay with surpassing providence... He set up a royal form clothed in glory (Ps 8:6), an image worthy of honor; He gave him features after the likeness of the Creator, since He willed it. Therefore it befits each one of us to keep this image at all times, and especially in time of trial... So now Job depicts precisely the whole history of Adam, giving us a brief teaching, which Moses explained at length.

10.8.11.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem. * Jonah was distressed after his flight and the reconciliation of the people of Nineveh with God... suffering and agitated in a human way, full of sorrow. So God commanded the earth to cause a gourd to grow for Jonah to shelter his head, then commanded the sun to increase its heat and scorch it. Jonah was angry at its perishing, but when the Lord comforted him and then tried him, hear what He says to him: [Thou hast had pity on the gourd, for the which thou hast not laboured, neither madest it grow; which came up in a night, and perished in a night: And should not I spare Nineveh, that great city, wherein are more than sixscore thousand persons that cannot discern between their right hand and their left hand?] (Jon 4:10-11).

10.8.12.en: This is what He wanted to say: Did you not rejoice in the shade of the gourd? How much more ought I to rejoice at the salvation of the people of Nineveh! Were you not pained at its perishing? So the perishing of humanity pains me...

10.8.13.en: He did not say to him: "You had pity on the gourd" and stop... but continued: "for the which thou hast not laboured, neither madest it grow." For just as the gardener has pity on the tree over which he has labored more than over others, so God wanted to establish His love for mankind through this love. It is as though He says to him: You defend strongly the work of another, in which you did not labor; how much more is it fitting for me to defend the work of my hands! Then He lessens the sharpness of the charge brought against them by saying: "that cannot discern between their right hand and their left hand," that is, they sinned without knowledge...

10.8.14.en: And He reproaches those who groan that they are forsaken, saying: "Concerning my sons, and concerning the work of my hands command ye me" (Isa 45:11), as though saying: Who reminds a father of his son or urges him to think of him? Or who reminds the artist not to spoil his art?!

10.8.15.en: St. John Chrysostom. Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that the earthy man bears an earthy mind that inclines to temporal earthly things, but the Holy Spirit lifts him up to heavenly things.

10.8.16.en: It is out of God's love that He withdraws the grace of His Holy Spirit from him, as it were, for a time, until he discovers his true state and cries out: "Wilt thou bring me into dust again?" [9]. Man feels his weakness and realizes that without the intervention of the breath of heavenly grace he is dry dust.

10.9.0.en: "Hast thou not poured me out as milk, and curdled me like cheese?" [10]

10.9.1.en: A wonderful comparison: as a simple person can pour milk or make cheese, so with ease and simplicity God made man.

10.9.2.en: * When the Lord took a body He was not ashamed of it, since He is the Former of bodies. But who told us this? The Lord says to Jeremiah: "Before I formed thee in the belly I knew thee; and before thou camest forth out of the womb I sanctified thee" (Jer 1:5). If He was not ashamed of creating the body of man, would He be ashamed of the body in which He hid His divinity, He who creates infants in the womb, as Job wrote: "Hast thou not poured me out as milk, and curdled me like cheese? Thou hast clothed me with skin and flesh, and hast fenced me with bones and sinews?"

10.9.3.en: St. Cyril of Jerusalem. Again, when the grace of the Holy Spirit works in it, our mind is drawn away from what it was, and our understanding becomes like poured milk, and is formed by the Holy Spirit anew into tenderness and gentleness, and becomes like a piece of cheese.

10.9.4.en: * The immortal rational nature is hidden in our worn-out body, and suggests by all its acts in it and through it. And so, since you have this body, which has become an altar on which incense is offered, place upon it all your thoughts and evil counsels before the face of the Lord, lifting up your minds and hearts to Him, beseeching Him to send His holy fire to burn up all that is on this altar and purify it; then your adversaries (the demons and sins), the priests of Baal, will fear you and perish at your hands, as happened with Elijah the prophet (1 Kgs 18:25 ff.). Then you will behold the Holy Comforter in the divine water (Baptism) that rains upon you a spiritual rain.

10.10.0.en: St. Anthony the Great. "Thou hast clothed me with skin and flesh, and hast fenced me with bones and sinews" [11].

10.10.1.en: When God created man, He did not create him naked, for He clothed him with skin; nor did He make him weak, for He knit him with bones and sinews. Thus our inner organs are clothed with skin and fortified with bones and nerves. Man could have lived in dignity and strength had sin not stripped him and weakened his power.

10.10.2.en: Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that the inner man is clothed with skin and flesh, because while rising toward heavenly things he finds at the same time an obstacle, being besieged by bodily movements that hinder him.

10.10.3.en: And St. John Chrysostom sees that Job touches upon the surpassing providence of God, who created him out of nothing and gave him skin and body, bones and sinews; how then could this Creator, so inventive in His love, care, and powers, fail to care for man, His beloved?

10.10.4.en: * He means: Are You not the One to whom he gives assurance of the greatness of love toward man and the greatness of this wisdom? If Job refers to the formation of man in some detail, it is only to prove that, after He created him out of nothing, He would deny this great providence of God and His surpassing wisdom? And he has shown that man (in himself) is nothing.

10.10.5.en: St. John Chrysostom. * He is a wise Maker indeed; who prepared the womb to bear the fetus?!

10.10.6.en: Who gives life to the lifeless things within you?!

10.10.7.en: Who bound us with muscles and bones, and clothed us with skin and flesh, and as soon as the child is born the milk overflows from the breasts?!

10.10.8.en: How does the child grow to be a boy, then a youth, then a man, and remain so until he passes into old age, without anyone noticing this subtle change from day to day?!

10.11.0.en: St. Cyril of Jerusalem. "Thou hast granted me life and favour, and thy visitation hath preserved my spirit" [12].

10.11.1.en: If we have anything to complain about, even of what comes from God, we resort to Him. He permits affliction so that we may learn to resort to Him, for He is the One who created us that we might enjoy Him, not that we might murmur.

10.11.2.en: Along with the gift of the body in the splendor of its creation and its visible and hidden capacities, God gave us something greater, namely the breath of life from the mouth of God. He granted us life and mercy, and gave us the grace of reason and thought along with heart and emotions.

10.11.3.en: He established the soul hidden in the body, but what keeps it is not the body with its powers and energies, but the providence of God.

10.11.4.en: * How powerful is this holy man's lament for the common weakness of all men! How heavy was the charge that God made man with His hands, and yet man offers an excuse for committing sin on the plea that he is weak, while grace declares the eternal work in us through the tenderness of heavenly protection.

10.11.5.en: St. Ambrose. * "And thy visitation hath preserved my spirit" [12]. It is not enough that you have this by nature, but it requires Your divine providence over us. He says: Throughout all my life I rely on Your divine providence.

10.11.6.en: * If you doubt God's providence, ask the earth and the heavens and the sun and the moon, ask the irrational creatures and the plants... Ask the rocks and the mountains, the sand dunes and the hills. Ask the night and the day. For God's providence is clearer than the sun and its rays. In every place, in the wilderness and in inhabited cities, on the earth and in the seas... wherever you go you hear a speaking testimony of this crying providence...

10.11.7.en: In every place voices rise resounding, clearer than the voices of rational men, proclaiming to everyone who wants to hear the watchful love of God!

10.11.8.en: And when the prophet wished to record the power of these voices he said: [Their line is gone out through all the earth, and their words to the end of the world] (Ps 19:4).

10.11.9.en: Our own language is understood only by the people of our tongue, but creation speaks a language that all peoples understand!

10.11.10.en: St. John Chrysostom. "And these things hast thou hid in thine heart."

10.12.0.en: "I know that this is with thee" [13].

10.12.1.en: Job was in a struggle between these free divine graces and God's surpassing care to preserve the body as well as the soul, and the unbearable troubles he was permitted to suffer. Therefore he says: "And these things hast thou hid in thine heart," that is, the two agree together through Your will hidden within You, whose depths none of us can fathom. He is certain both of God's providence and of God's permitting him to suffer: "I know that this is with thee."

10.12.2.en: * [Since You have hidden these in Yourself, I know that You can do all things, and nothing is impossible for You](أ). Do you not see that the possibility of knowing God is revealed in His creation (Rev 1:19); it is enough for my creation to show me God's existence and power, without need of heaven? For since we were created thus, to exist from a seed, and to be under this help, and not to be allowed to fall into dangers, all this suffices to show God's power and authority. Likewise in the fact of the sinner's being preserved and not punished (here), and in the righteous man's being disciplined and punished.

10.12.3.en: St. John Chrysostom. * How could such a thing (granting life and mercy) not belong to such a Creator?

10.12.4.en: What could be impossible for Him?

10.12.5.en: If You made the clay in the image of God (Gen 2:7), and made the dust pass to the rank of a rational being, if You give earthly beings a happiness equal to that of heavenly beings, how could You not work a miracle for me?

10.13.0.en: 14 If I sin, then thou markest me, and thou wilt not acquit me from mine iniquity. 15 If I be wicked, woe unto me; and if I be righteous, yet will I not lift up my head. I am full of confusion; therefore see thou mine affliction; 16 For it increaseth. Thou huntest me as a fierce lion: and again thou shewest thyself marvellous upon me. 17 Thou renewest thy witnesses against me, and increasest thine indignation upon me; changes and war are against me.

10.13.1.en: "If I sin, then thou markest me, and thou wilt not acquit me from mine iniquity" [14].

10.13.2.en: Job does not deny that he is mistaken, and that God knows his sins and marks them, and by this Job will not be justified before Him. "If thou, LORD, shouldest mark iniquities, O Lord, who shall stand?" (Ps 130:3)

10.13.3.en: * If I sin, You mark me, lest I fall into the pit (Ps 28:1), into the utmost sin, and be utterly lost, and lest I stray from the flock (Jn 10:1) and go to the den of wolves. According to the law of justice You do not find me righteous, but find me blameworthy under the stroke of the inherited curse (Gen 3:17).

10.13.4.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem. Job realized that he could not be justified by himself, but needs the One who grants it. Like all the fathers of the Old Testament he was longing for the coming of the Messiah, the Savior.

10.13.5.en: * The Lord Christ suffered at the time when Pontius Pilate was acting as governor and judge...

10.13.6.en: Who suffered? Our Lord, the only-begotten Son of God!

10.13.7.en: And what happened to Him? He was crucified, died, and was buried!

10.13.8.en: And for whom? For the wicked and sinners!

10.13.9.en: How great is this condescension! How great is the grace!

10.13.10.en: "What shall I render unto the LORD for all his benefits toward me?" (Ps 116:12).

10.13.11.en: St. Augustine. * Christ appears to each one according to his need. To those who need joy He comes as a vine; to those who need to be in the presence of the Father He comes as a door; those who need someone to offer their prayers find Him the Intercessor, the High Priest within them; and to sinners He is the Lamb (slain) for their sanctification.

10.13.12.en: He is all things to everyone without His nature changing, but remains as He is. He remains, and the work of His sonship will not change, but He adapts Himself to our weakness, being an excellent physician or a teacher full of tenderness. He is the Lord Himself; He did not receive lordship by advancement, but the work of His sonship is natural.

10.13.13.en: * The word "Jesus" means "Savior," and in Greek it means "the Healer," for He is the physician of souls and bodies, the healer of spirits; He opened the eyes of the man born blind, and led minds to the light. He heals the visibly lame, and leads sinners in the way of repentance. He says to the paralytic: "Sin no more," and also: "Take up thy bed, and walk" (Jn 5:14, 8), because the body was paralyzed by the sin of the soul. He ministered to the soul first so that healing might extend to the body.

10.13.14.en: Therefore if any of you is suffering in his soul from sins, you will find Him a physician for you. And if any of you is of little faith, let him say to Him: "Help thou mine unbelief" (Mk 9:24).

10.13.15.en: And if bodily pains afflict any of you, let him not be unbelieving but draw near, for Jesus heals such diseases, and let him know that Jesus is the Christ.

10.13.16.en: St. Cyril of Jerusalem. * Often the mind is disturbed in its depths at the remembrance of sin, and so urges its practice in a worse form than it had when it was first committed.

10.13.18.en: * "If I sin, then thou markest me" (Job 10:14). Confess your sins, O man, that you may obtain forgiveness: "Declare thou thy iniquities first, that thou mayest be justified" (Isa 43:26) LXX.

10.13.19.en: Why are you ashamed to confess them, when you were born in them? (Ps 51:5). He who denies his guilt and does not confess it in truth denies his birth.

10.13.20.en: But do you want to keep what you have received? Why do you think you possess what you have not received? Therefore let the sinner and the unholy confess, and let the righteous not exalt himself nor be proud, lest he lose the reward of his righteousness through pride (Job 10:15).

10.13.21.en: St. Ambrose. "If I be wicked, woe unto me."

10.13.22.en: "And if I be righteous, yet will I not lift up my head."

10.14.0.en: "I am full of confusion; therefore see thou mine affliction" [15].

10.14.1.en: Without repentance we fall into this woe to which Job refers here. For nothing can rescue me from it, neither moral loftiness nor my worship, whatever it may be, as long as it is without repentance. This is what Job means by saying: "If I be righteous," that is, if I rely on my self-righteousness or on my conduct or service, all this will not lift up my head before my God.

10.14.2.en: The Holy Bible warns us against sin of any kind, for it brings shame and dishonor: "I am full of confusion; therefore see thou mine affliction" [15].

10.14.3.en: "Righteousness exalteth a nation: but sin is a reproach to any people" (Prov 14:34).

10.14.4.en: "Have mercy upon us, O LORD, have mercy upon us: for we are exceedingly filled with contempt" (Ps 123:3).

10.14.5.en: "The wise shall inherit glory: but shame shall be the promotion of fools" (Prov 3:35).

10.14.6.en: "When pride cometh, then cometh shame: but with the lowly is wisdom" (Prov 11:2).

10.14.7.en: "Poverty and shame shall be to him that refuseth instruction: but he that regardeth reproof shall be honoured" (Prov 13:18).
